subChunks.title: Set Implementations

storyBeats.text: Eldrin empties a bag of magical crystals onto the table — many are identical. He slides them all into a glowing ring that rejects any duplicate that enters.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A Set is the uncompromising collector — it will not hold two identical items. When uniqueness is a requirement, a Set enforces it automatically, with no effort on your part. A HashSet does it fastest; a TreeSet keeps them sorted.

storyBeats.label: HashSet and TreeSet

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: For equals() and hashCode() to work correctly in a HashSet, your objects must implement both. This is why we overrode them earlier — the collection depends on those contracts.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a HashSet<String> from the list ["alpha", "beta", "alpha", "gamma", "beta"]. Print the size (should be 3). Then create a TreeSet from the same list and print it (sorted).
guidedPractice.hint: Pass the list to the HashSet constructor: new HashSet<>(items). Same for TreeSet.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet. When would you choose each?

questions.prompt: You need to track unique visitor IP addresses and quickly check if an IP has been seen before. Which collection is best?
questions.explanation: HashSet provides O(1) contains() and automatically rejects duplicates — ideal for unique membership tracking.
TreeSet deduplicates (5 → 4 unique values) and sorts. first() returns the smallest: 1.

subChunks.title: Queue, Deque & Map Variants

storyBeats.text: Eldrin directs the Academy queue of apprentices: 'First in, first seen by the Sorting Hat.' Then he demonstrates the priority queue — the highest-priority tasks are always handled first.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Different shapes of data demand different shapes of container. A queue for task processing; a priority queue when some tasks matter more; a deque when you need both ends; a TreeMap when your keys must always be sorted.

storyBeats.label: PriorityQueue demo

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The merge() method on Map is one of the most underrated additions in Java 8. For building frequency maps — counting how often each key appears — it replaces a four-line pattern with one line.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a PriorityQueue<Integer> with values [4, 1, 3, 2, 5]. Poll all elements and print each on a new line (they should come out in ascending order).
guidedPractice.hint: PriorityQueue polls the smallest element first. Use a while (!pq.isEmpty()) loop.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is the difference between Queue and Deque? When would you use a PriorityQueue?

questions.prompt: Which method adds to a Queue and returns false on failure (instead of throwing)?
questions.explanation: offer() is the safe Queue method — returns false if full. add() throws an exception. Use offer()/poll()/peek() for Queue operations.

subChunks.title: Collections Utility Class & Immutable Collections

storyBeats.text: Eldrin opens the Collections grimoire — a compendium of algorithms that no wizard should ever rewrite.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The Collections utility class is your shortcut to dozens of common algorithms. Sort, reverse, shuffle, min, max, frequency — all written by engineers far more patient than either of us. Use them.

storyBeats.label: Collections utilities

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And immutable collections — List.of(), Map.of() — are the sealed scrolls of the data world. Once created, they cannot be altered. They cost less memory, are thread-safe, and announce loudly: this data is fixed by design.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create an ArrayList of [5, 2, 8, 1, 9]. Sort it using Collections.sort() and print. Then print the maximum using Collections.max().
guidedPractice.hint: Collections.sort(nums) sorts in-place. Collections.max(nums) returns the largest element.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is the difference between List.of() and new ArrayList()? Why would you choose an immutable collection?

questions.prompt: What happens when you call add() on a list created with List.of()?
options: Creates a new list with the element
questions.explanation: List.of() creates an immutable list. Any attempt to modify it — add, remove, or set — throws UnsupportedOperationException.
